Content:
The graph has infinitely many asymptotes, and there is an infinite number of points where the function takes values of [MATH: 1] and [MATH: -1.] We can write down general expressions for these properties, by assuming [MATH: n] represents an integer.

Content:
The Asymptotes of the Function

Content:
The function has asymptotes when [MATH: x=\pm \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots,] etc. Therefore, a general equation for the asymptotes of the graph is

Content:
[MATH: x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi.]

Content:
The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of [MATH: \mathbf{1}]

Content:
From the graph, we see that the function takes a value of [MATH: 1] when [MATH: x=0.] Since the function has a period of [MATH: 2\pi,] a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] for which [MATH: \sec x = 1] is
[MATH: x = 2n\pi.]

Content:
The Points Where the Function Takes a Value of [MATH: \mathbf{-1}]

Content:
Similarly, from the graph, we see that the function takes a value of [MATH: -1] when [MATH: x=\pi.] Since the function has a period [MATH: 2\pi,] a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] for which [MATH: \sec x = -1] is
[MATH: x = \pi +2n\pi.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's have a look at the graph of [MATH: y=\sec x.]

  • The secant takes the value [MATH: 1] at [MATH: x = 2 n\pi .] Therefore, statement I is true.

  • The range of [MATH: f(x) = \sec x] is [MATH: (-\infty,-1] \cup [1, \infty)]. Therefore, statement II is false.

  • The secant graph does not intersect the [MATH: x]-axis. Therefore, statement III is false.

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \sec x =2 \sqrt 2] then what is [MATH: \sec(x+8\pi)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \sec x =2 \sqrt 2] then what is [MATH: \sec(x+8\pi)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y = \sec x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \sec{x} = \sec{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=4] into the above gives

[MATH: \sec x|= \sec (x + 2 ⋅ 4 ⋅ π); = \sec (x + 8π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \sec{x} = 2\sqrt 2,] then [MATH: \sec{(x+8\pi)} = 2\sqrt 2.]

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if it satisfies the property

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = f(x).]

Content:
As it turns out, secant is an even function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \sec(-x) = \sec(x).]

Content:
Even functions are always symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis. This is indeed true of the secant function, as we can see from the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8a10c2a399768b203591388f6c334d7e]

Content:
We can use the evenness property of secant in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example.

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \sec{x} = -\dfrac{11}{6},] then [MATH: \sec(-x - 14\pi) =]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \sec{x} = -\dfrac{11}{6},] then [MATH: \sec(-x - 14\pi) =]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \sec{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \sec{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]

  • Our graph is symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis. This means that [MATH: \sec{x}] is an even function, and we have [MATH: \sec(-x) = \sec{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \sec{x},] we have [MATH: \sec (− x − 14π)|= \sec (− x − 2π ⋅ 7); = \sec (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the evenness of [MATH: \sec{x},] we have [MATH: \sec (− x)|= \sec x; = − (11)/(6).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sec(-x - 14\pi) = -\dfrac{11}{6}.]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Secant Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \sec{x} = -\dfrac{11}{6},] then [MATH: \sec(-x - 14\pi) =]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \sec{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/54de4a90efd6ebeccfdace7b62890f94]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \sec{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]
- Our graph is symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis. This means that [MATH: \sec{x}] is an even function, and we have
[MATH: \sec(-x) = \sec{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \sec{x},] we have
[MATH: \sec (− x − 14π)|= \sec (− x − 2π ⋅ 7); = \sec (− x).]
- Secondly, using the evenness of [MATH: \sec{x},] we have
[MATH: \sec (− x)|= \sec x; = − (11)/(6).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sec(-x - 14\pi) = -\dfrac{11}{6}.]
